Louis XIV. From 1638 to 1715, he was called the Sun King. He was the longest-reigning European monarch and the embodiment of absolute monarchy. He centralized royal power, built Versailles as the ultimate seat of government, and made France the dominant military and cultural force in Europe.

His reign lasted 72 years, from 1643 to 1715, the longest documented reign of any European sovereign. He assumed personal rule in 1661 after Cardinal Mazarin's death, and from that moment he was the state incarnate. He declared himself in the words that became his motto: I am the state. This embodied the divine-right absolutism that defined his reign and influenced monarchs across Europe.

His most enduring monument was the Palace of Versailles, built outside Paris as a vast architectural statement. It became the seat of government and the place where the nobility were compelled to attend him daily. The palace symbolized his power and the grandeur of France. Ministers, generals, and aristocrats all gathered at Versailles, bound to his person and dependent on his favor.

Louis took the sun as his personal symbol, representing the divine source of all life and power radiating from himself as king. The courtiers who orbited around him were not centers of power but planets orbiting the sun. He patronized the arts and sciences lavishly. The court at Versailles became the model for elegance and culture across Europe, setting standards that other monarchs emulated.

Yet his reign contained contradictions and costs. In 1685 he revoked the Edict of Nantes, ending religious tolerance for Protestants and triggering the flight of Huguenots, which weakened France economically. He waged numerous wars of expansion, including the War of Spanish Succession, extending French borders but leaving the treasury depleted by his death. The grandeur had its price.
